span.label: existence
span.quote: Without such a 3D base, 2D materials were presumed not to exist until 2004, when the common wisdom was flaunted by the experimental discovery of graphene7 and other free-standing 2D atomic crystals (for example, single-layer boron nitride and half-layer BSCCO)8.

span.label: graphene (two-dimensional atomic crystals)
span.quote: Graphene is the name given to a flat monolayer of carbon atoms tightly packed into a two-dimensional (2D) honeycomb lattice, and is a basic building block for graphitic materials of all other dimensionalities (Figure 1).

span.label: review
span.quote: Before reviewing the earlier work on graphene, it is useful to define what 2D crystals are.

span.label: Because QED effects scale inversely with the speed of light, replacing c by the Fermi velocity enhances them in graphene by about 300.

span.quote: QED-specific phenomena are often inversely proportional to the speed of light c and, therefore, enhanced in graphene by a factor c/vF ≈300

span.label: The electronic structure evolves with layer number and reaches the 3D graphite limit at about ten layers, which makes the 2D/3D boundary operational rather than stipulated.

span.label: The relativistic vocabulary is a description, not a claim about the physics - the paper says so itself while adopting it.

The concepts of chirality and pseudospin are important because many electronic processes in graphene can be understood as due to conservation of these quantities

span.label: contradicts → Landau's and Peierls' argument that strictly two-dimensional crystals are thermodynamically unstable and cannot exist
span.quote: More than 70 years ago, Landau and Peierls argued that strictly two-dimensional (2D) crystals were thermodynamically unstable and could not exist11,12. Their theory pointed out that a divergent contribution of thermal fluctuations in low-dimensional crystal lattices should lead to such displacements of atoms that they become comparable to interatomic distances at any finite temperature13. The argument was later extended by Mermin14 and is strongly supported by a whole omnibus of experimental observations. Indeed, the melting temperature of thin films rapidly decreases with decreasing thickness, and they become unstable (segregate into islands or decompose) at a thickness of, typically, dozens of atomic layers15,16. For this reason, atomic monolayers have so far been known only as an integral part of larger 3D structures, usually grown epitaxially on top of monocrystals with matching crystal lattices15,16. Without such a 3D base, 2D materials were presumed not to exist until 2004, when the common wisdom was flaunted by the experimental discovery of graphene7 and other free-standing 2D atomic crystals (for example, single-layer boron nitride and half-layer BSCCO)8.

span.label: reinterprets → the categorical boundary between a 2D crystal and a thin 3D film
span.note: The paper replaces a stipulated boundary with a measured one and then divides the resulting class into three, on the same criterion.
span.quote: This allows one to distinguish between single-, double- and few- (3 to <10) layer graphene as three different types of 2D crystals

span.quote: This requires an index to indicate sublattices A and B, which is similar to the spin index (up and down) in QED and, therefore, is referred to as pseudospin. Accordingly, in the formal description of graphene’s quasiparticles by the Dirac-like Hamiltonian above, σr refers to pseudospin rather than the real spin of electrons (the latter must be described by additional terms in the Hamiltonian
